title: Malibu's Most Wanted
full_review:
An overprivileged white kid from the California coast who fancies himself as a self-styled rapper gets a dose of urban reality in the mindless satire, "Malibu's Most Wanted" (Warner Bros.).

Directed by John Whitesell, the film, a vapid jumble of mildly amusing comedy sketches, is a misguided attempt to comment on the puzzling sociological phenomenon of silver-spoon youths' fascination with the subculture of gangsta rap.

Brad "B-Rad" Gluckman (Jamie Kennedy) hails from the "mean streets" of Malibu. According to Brad, life in the "'Bu" is hard core, in spite of its manicured lawns and haute-couture boutiques. During the opening sequence viewers are educated to life in the 'hood, with Kennedy's mockingly-grave voice intoned over images of privilege, including a bunch of rich kids mugging it in faux-gang colors -- the ACCs (Abused Children of Celebrities).

Brad's father, Bill Gluckman (Ryan O'Neal), is a high-profile politician, running for governor of California. Obviously, his black-sheep, hip-hop son poses a public relations nightmare. The well-intentioned Brad offers to help with the campaign, but his ghetto sensibilities cause a stir with Gluckman's white-bread constituency and result in a dramatic plunge in his standings.

With therapy proving ineffective in curing Brad's embarrassing "ghettophrenia," Bill's campaign manager (Blair Underwood) recommends Bill take a more drastic approach. He suggests staging a carjacking, using actors (Taye Diggs and Anthony Anderson) posing as thugs, in which Brad will be kidnapped and held for ransom in the heart of violence-riddled South Central Los Angeles -- hopefully once and for all scaring the "black" out of him.

The plan, of course, backfires, as the bumbling, classically-trained thespians find themselves in over their heads. They enlist the help of Shondra (Regina Hall), a streetwise, business-savvy beauty who actually lives in the 'hood. Brad quickly falls for her ghetto charm, which does not sit well with her gang-banging ex-boyfriend. In the end, Brad's father comes to his son's rescue -- both realizing that the mutual love they share transcends their differences.

Based on a character featured regularly on Kennedy's WB network show, "The Jamie Kennedy Experiment", the film is little more than a catalogue of lewd ghetto cliches that quickly grow stale. "Malibu" never evolves past Kennedy's hip-hop shtick to postulate on the deeper question posed: why the rap life-style of inner-city youths is so alluring to their affluent counterparts.

The scenes with Diggs and Anderson prove to be the only dividends paid. Their pretentious method-acting tiffs play against racial stereotypes and make for some genuinely comic moments. The hypocrisy of empty campaign promises, slickly marketed to garner low-income votes, is also lampooned effectively.

Despite the crassness of much of the humor, the film, to its credit, does not glamorize the drugs and violence prevalent in other films dealing with the rap subculture.

Due to an instance of rough language, recurring obscenities and lewd sexual humor and violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
